name: reckless
workload: Single-threaded periodic logging calls, a buffer-filling 'call burst' scenario, and a disk-I/O-bound scenario (2048 log entries interleaved with writing 64GiB of data), timing reckless against std::fstream, fprintf/stdio, spdlog, g3log, and Boost.Log.
claimed_speedup: Periodic calls: relative avg latency 1.00 (reckless) vs 41.32 (fstream) vs 43.77 (stdio) vs 40.85 (spdlog); call burst: 1.00 vs 2.36 (fstream) vs 2.55 (stdio); disk I/O: 1.00 (reckless) vs 17.01 (stdio) [fstream not included in this scenario]
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0; exact optimization flags not stated on the benchmark page
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X @ 3.7GHz, 8 cores (SMT off); Samsung 970 EVO 1TB SSD (+ WD Red 3TB HDD for disk-I/O scenario); 32GB RAM; Linux kernel 4.14.65
tradeoffs: Async design allows passing raw pointers to the background writer thread for speed, at the cost of dangling-pointer risk if misused; trades some floating-point formatting precision for performance; writes are backgrounded/batched rather than immediate, with a configurable buffer size trading latency spikes against memory use.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own doc/performance.md and benchmarks/*.cpp); per the evidence-tier rules a first-party benchmark with partial methodology is capped at C even though hardware and compiler are unusually well documented here — the exact optimization flags used are not stated. GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION for the repo, but LICENSE.txt contains standard MIT license text with only a custom header, so it is recorded as MIT. No commits since October 2023.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "github quill logging library benchmark faster than fprintf std::cout" surfaced mattiasflodin/reckless via a comparison table in odygrd/quill's README; opened reckless/doc/performance.md and repo metadata directly via gh api

name: FastReader
workload: Reading a file line-by-line with a custom WinAPI-backed CFileHandler iterator vs. std::ifstream, timed via a Google Test benchmark (one run shown in the README).
claimed_speedup: CFileHandler: 56,700 ns vs std::ifstream: 241,000 ns -- about 4.25x faster (project describes this as 'almost 5 times faster')
tradeoffs: Windows-only (WinAPI-based); narrower API than std::ifstream (line iteration only, wide-char paths); GPL-3.0 is copyleft, which may be unsuitable for proprietary use.
caveats: Numbers come from a single test run shown in the README with no stated compiler, optimization flags, CPU model, or repeat/averaging methodology. Small, single-maintainer project with no commits since November 2019.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than std::ifstream"

name: CPath
baseline: find (GNU findutils), TinyDir, Cute Files, Python os.walk
workload: Recursive vs. explicit-stack directory traversal over a large synthetic directory tree (C API and C++ bindings), averaged over 100 runs, measuring user/system/wall time, compared against `find`, Python os.walk, Cute Files, and TinyDir.
claimed_speedup: Wall time 0.082-0.083s for CPath (recursion/emplace, C and C++) vs 0.147s for `find`, 0.237s for Python os.walk, 0.284s for Cute Files, 0.294s for TinyDir -- roughly 1.8x faster than `find` and ~3.5x faster than TinyDir/Cute Files (project describes this as 'often around 3x faster than other libraries and even faster than find')
compiler_and_flags: -O3 (project states -O1/-O2 give the same result; -O0 is ~5% slower); compiler name not stated
hardware: MacBook Air7,2, Intel Core i5 @ 1.6GHz, 2 cores, 256KB L2 cache/core, 3MB L3, 8GB RAM
tradeoffs: C89/C99-era API by design for broad pre-C++17 compiler support; larger codebase (~2.5k lines) than minimal alternatives like TinyDir/Cute Files; does not eagerly load stat() info (opt-in), trading a feature for speed; author explicitly states CPath is 'NOT a replacement for a more heavy duty library like std::filesystem.'
caveats: The published benchmark compares against `find`, TinyDir, Cute Files, and Python os.walk -- not against std::filesystem directly -- and the README explicitly disclaims being a std::filesystem replacement, so this is reported as evidence against a related-but-different incumbent (baseline_in_list=false) with lower confidence for the stdlib-replacement framing. Benchmark is first-party and single-machine, and no compiler name is given.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "faster than std::filesystem github library benchmark directory traversal"
